topic: CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1201) exam preparation - mobile devices, networking, hardware, virtualization and cloud computing, and hardware and network troubleshooting
exam_format: Maximum of 90 questions in 90 minutes, delivered at Pearson VUE test centers or online-proctored. Question types include multiple choice (single and multiple response), drag-and-drop, and performance-based questions (PBQs) that simulate real tasks. Scored 100-900 with a passing score of 675 for Core 1. This is the current V15 exam (220-1201), which launched March 25, 2025 and replaced 220-1101, with an estimated retirement around 2028 - tell candidates to verify the current exam version and objectives on CompTIA's official site before scheduling. To earn the full CompTIA A+ certification a candidate must pass BOTH Core 1 (220-1201) and Core 2 (220-1202). Exam fee is approximately USD 259 per exam (varies by region and voucher; bundles exist) - present it as approximate and advise confirming current CompTIA pricing. The certification is valid for three years and can be renewed through CompTIA's continuing-education program.
question_types: multiple choice (single answer, exactly 4 options) and multiple response clearly marked 'Select TWO/THREE', plus scenario items modeled on the exam's performance-based tasks; every item is a practical support scenario asking which device, port, protocol, component, or troubleshooting step is correct - NOT rote definitions
audience: Aspiring and early-career IT support and help-desk technicians, field service technicians, and desktop support specialists. CompTIA recommends about 9-12 months of hands-on experience in a help-desk, desktop, or field role, though no formal prerequisite is required. A foundational entry point into IT that pairs naturally with the CompTIA Network+ (N10-009) and Security+ (SY0-701) courses already in this catalog - A+ is the recommended first step of the CompTIA trifecta.
author: Aseem Mankotia

domains.name: Mobile Devices
domains.notes: Installing and configuring laptop hardware and components (batteries, keyboards, storage, memory, wireless cards, biometrics) and display components; configuring and using mobile-device features and network connectivity/application support (cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, hotspot, NFC, mobile device management/MDM concepts, synchronization and email configuration - IMAP/POP3/SMTP, ports, and security settings). Choosing the correct mobile component, connection type, or configuration for a described scenario, and distinguishing laptop vs mobile-specific hardware.

domains.name: Networking
domains.notes: Comparing TCP and UDP ports, protocols, and their purposes (e.g., 20/21 FTP, 22 SSH, 23 Telnet, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 67/68 DHCP, 80 HTTP, 110 POP3, 137-139/445 SMB/NetBIOS, 143 IMAP, 161/162 SNMP, 389 LDAP, 443 HTTPS, 3389 RDP); networking hardware (routers, switches, access points, firewalls, cables and connectors); wireless standards and technologies (Wi-Fi generations, frequencies, encryption); configuring TCP/IP (IPv4/IPv6 addressing, subnets, DHCP, DNS, APIPA, static vs dynamic); Internet connection types; and network services/SOHO setup. Choosing the correct port, protocol, connector, or configuration for a described scenario.

domains.name: Hardware
domains.notes: The heaviest knowledge domain. Identifying and using cables and connectors; installing and configuring motherboards, CPUs, RAM (DDR generations, ECC), and add-on cards; power supplies (wattage, connectors, efficiency); storage devices (HDD, SSD, NVMe, M.2, RAID levels 0/1/5/10); peripherals; and printers (laser imaging process, inkjet, thermal, 3D, configuration and maintenance, print servers). Choosing the correct component, cable/connector, RAID level, or printer type/setting for a described scenario.

domains.name: Virtualization and Cloud Computing
domains.notes: Summarizing cloud-computing concepts (cloud models - public/private/hybrid/community; service models - IaaS/PaaS/SaaS; shared resources, measured service, rapid elasticity, high availability, file synchronization, virtual desktops/DaaS) and setting up and configuring client-side virtualization (hypervisors, resource requirements, purposes such as sandboxing/test dev, security requirements). Choosing the correct cloud model, service model, or virtualization approach for a described scenario, and distinguishing IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS.

domains.name: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting
domains.notes: The largest domain. Applying the CompTIA best-practice troubleshooting methodology (identify the problem; establish a theory of probable cause; test the theory; establish a plan of action; verify full system functionality and implement preventive measures; document findings, actions, and outcomes) and troubleshooting common problems with motherboards/CPU/RAM/power, storage drives and RAID arrays, video/display and projectors, mobile-device components, printers, and wired/wireless networks. Choosing the correct next troubleshooting step or most likely cause for a described symptom - emphasize the methodology ORDER, which the exam tests heavily.

extra_guidance: CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1201) is the current V15 Core 1 exam (launched March 25, 2025, replacing 220-1101) and is the recommended first credential of the CompTIA trifecta alongside the Network+ (N10-009) and Security+ (SY0-701) courses in this catalog. To earn the full A+ certification a candidate must pass BOTH Core 1 (220-1201) and Core 2 (220-1202) - state this clearly and note this course covers Core 1 only, with a companion Core 2 course available. The exam is scenario- and task-based, including performance-based questions (PBQs) - the real skill it tests is 'given this support situation, which device, port, protocol, component, or troubleshooting step is correct,' NOT memorizing definitions; model practice items on realistic support scenarios rather than trivia. This is a vendor-neutral, READ-AND-UNDERSTAND support course - explain the concepts, ports, connectors, and step-by-step procedures rather than requiring specific hardware; keep it hands-on in spirit with concrete examples. Cover the exam's signature emphases exactly: the standard port/protocol table (memorize the common ports listed in the Networking domain notes), RAID levels and storage interfaces (SATA, NVMe, M.2), DDR memory generations and ECC, the laser-printer imaging process in order (processing, charging, exposing, developing, transferring, fusing, cleaning), IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS and cloud models, client-side virtualization purposes, and - most important - the SIX-STEP CompTIA troubleshooting methodology in the correct order (the exam tests the order, and the final step is always 'document findings, actions, and outcomes'). Flag classic traps: TCP vs UDP for a given service, POP3 vs IMAP, HTTP vs HTTPS and RDP ports, RAID 5 vs RAID 10, and 'always verify before documenting.' Use current terminology and note technology evolves, so verify against CompTIA's current objectives. The five domain names and weights above are CompTIA's official 220-1201 exam-objective weights (Mobile Devices 13%, Networking 23%, Hardware 25%, Virtualization and Cloud Computing 11%, Hardware and Network Troubleshooting 28%) - use them verbatim. NEVER promise a pass or use the word 'guarantee' in ANY form (Udemy compliance) - use 'exam-focused preparation' framing throughout, including learning objectives and who-this-is-for. Present the exam fee as approximate (~USD 259 per exam, varies by region; bundles exist) and note the 3-year validity with CompTIA continuing education. The final chapter must be a full exam simulation with a 90-minute, up-to-90-question time-management strategy that accounts for performance-based questions (PBQs). Scan the practice bank for stray other-vendor/cloud-specific terms before upload per the pipeline compliance rules.
